approachQuestion.prompt:
Longest Segment Within Budget

The array `costs` gives the non-negative cost of each consecutive stage. Return the greatest number of consecutive stages whose total cost is at most `budget`. The segment must be contiguous. Return 0 if every single stage costs more than the budget. Leave the input unchanged.

Limits and assumptions:
• 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 0 ≤ costs[i] ≤ 10^9; 0 ≤ budget ≤ 10^12.
• Costs are non-negative and may be zero; sums fit in a 64-bit integer.
• Return only the segment length.

Examples:
1. costs = [4,0,2,0,3,1], budget = 5 → 4, for [0,2,0,3].
2. costs = [6,0,0], budget = 5 → 2, for [0,0].
3. costs = [], budget = 0 → 0.

Choose one approach.
constraints: Costs are non-negative and may be zero; sums fit in a 64-bit integer.

options.text: Extend the window to the right. When its sum exceeds the budget, remove costs from the left until the condition holds again. Then update the greatest length.
options.feedback: Removing a non-negative cost cannot increase the sum. Once a segment exceeds the budget, any longer segment with the same start also exceeds it.

options.text: Use binary search to find the greatest length L for which some length-L segment costs at most the budget. Check each trial length with one fixed-length moving window.
options.feedback: This is correct: with non-negative costs, a valid length-L segment contains a valid segment of every shorter length. Rechecking the full array for each trial is unnecessary when one variable-length window can track the best segment.

options.text: Sort the costs from smallest to largest and add the cheapest values while their sum stays within the budget. Return how many were chosen.
options.feedback: The selected positions may not be contiguous. For [1,100,1,1] with budget 3, this selects three ones, but the longest valid contiguous segment has length 2.

options.text: When the current segment exceeds the budget, discard the whole segment and start a new window after its right boundary.
options.feedback: The end of the current segment may still be a valid candidate. For [2,2,1] with budget 3, [2,1] has length 2, but resetting after [2,2] can miss it.

feedback.reason: Check how non-negative costs affect the sum when the window grows or shrinks.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the method “Extend the window and shrink it whenever the sum exceeds the budget,” choose one pair: running time and additional space.
constraints: Analyze only the named method. Do not count the input or returned value as additional space.
There is no recursion or call stack.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(1) additional space

feedback.reason: Both boundaries move only to the right, and each position enters and leaves the window at most once. The method keeps the sum and the best length.

details.correctness: Because costs are non-negative, extending the window cannot decrease its sum, and removing the leftmost cost cannot increase it. When the sum exceeds the budget, move the left boundary to the first position that restores validity; any longer segment with the same start also exceeds the budget. Zeros preserve these directions, though the left boundary may need several moves.
details.alternatives: Binary search over the length is correct because feasibility is monotone across lengths, but it makes several full passes. Sorting breaks contiguity. Resetting the whole window discards valid suffixes that could be part of the best segment.

methodReveal.title: A longest valid window with non-negative costs
methodReveal.description: Add stages from the right and keep their total cost. While the total exceeds the budget, remove the cost at the left boundary. When the condition holds, compare the current length with the best length.
